item.title: Capella Sydney Deepens Its Place in the City With a Second MICHELIN Key
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Capella Sydney has been awarded Two MICHELIN Keys for 2026, becoming the only hotel in Sydney to receive the distinction this year and advancing from One MICHELIN Key in 2025. The recognition comes during a particularly strong period for the hotel, which was also named No. 16 on The World’s 50 Best Hotels 2026 list and Best Hotel in Oceania for the second consecutive year. Together, the accolades reflect a property that has quickly established an identity rooted not simply in luxury, but in design, hospitality and a strong connection to Sydney.

That sense of place begins with the building itself. Capella Sydney occupies the heritage-listed former Department of Education building in the city’s Sandstone Precinct, where original architectural details are paired with contemporary Australian design and a collection of more than 1,400 artworks. Since opening in 2023, the hotel has extended that connection through its dining, wellness and cultural offerings, including Brasserie 1930, McRae Bar, Auriga Spa and its Culturists, who introduce guests to the people, places and stories that shape the city.

The Curated Take: The second MICHELIN Key is significant because Capella Sydney is no longer simply a beautifully restored historic building with a new luxury hotel inside it. The property has had several years to establish how it interprets Sydney through art, architecture, hospitality and access to the city, making this recognition feel more like an acknowledgment of an emerging Sydney institution than a debut accolade.

item.title: The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo Turns Reef Restoration Into Part of the Guest Experience
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The Westin Maldives Miriandhoo Resort has begun a new chapter in marine conservation with Coral RISE, a coral restoration initiative on its house reef in Baa Atoll. The first phase, completed in September, installed 100 Reef Stars carrying 1,500 coral fragments using the MARS Assisted Reef Restoration System, a science-based approach designed to provide damaged reef areas with a stable foundation for coral growth and marine habitat. The project is being developed with MARS Sustainable Solutions and will continue with monitoring and maintenance as the reef develops.

What distinguishes the initiative is its connection to the guest experience. The restoration site is accessible for snorkeling, allowing visitors to observe the Reef Stars and follow the progress of the coral over time, while marine education introduces guests to the importance of reef ecosystems in the Maldives. The project also complements the resort’s broader sustainability efforts and its location within the UNESCO Biosphere Reserve of Baa Atoll, where the surrounding marine environment is central to the destination itself.

The Curated Take: Coral RISE moves conservation from something a resort promotes to something guests can actually see taking shape. That creates a different relationship with the destination: rather than simply enjoying the reef, travelers have an opportunity to understand the work involved in helping restore it and to return to see how that effort evolves.

item.title: The Nam Hai Creates a Vietnamese Take on the Festive Season
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Four Seasons Resort The Nam Hai in Hoi An, the festive season takes on a distinctly Vietnamese character. From December 22, 2026 through January 1, 2027, the all-villa resort will combine familiar holiday traditions with experiences rooted in Central Vietnam, from the Thap Nen candle-lighting ceremony and an Enchanted Chocolate Garden exploring Vietnam’s cacao traditions to Christmas dining and a Midnight Forest New Year’s Eve celebration beneath the tropical canopy. The setting, with private pools, gardens and views of the sea, allows families and friends to move between celebration and quiet time at their own pace.

The season also extends beyond the resort itself, with Hoi An Ancient Town, My Son Sanctuary and the Imperial City of Hue offering access to the region’s layered cultural heritage. Guests can explore Hoi An by Vespa, visit a fishing village by bamboo basket boat or incorporate seasonal wellness into their stay at the lotus-filled Heart of the Earth Spa, where new Khoi Sac treatments draw on Vietnamese traditions of renewal. Private villas, including the three-bedroom ocean-view option, provide a residential setting for multigenerational gatherings while preserving space for individual retreat.

The Curated Take: The appeal here is less about recreating a conventional Christmas in a tropical setting and more about allowing the holiday season to become part of the destination. Vietnamese rituals, Central Vietnam’s cultural heritage, local ingredients and the resort’s distinctive coastal setting give familiar celebrations a sense of place.

item.title: Hotel Mulia Senayan’s 2026 Tripadvisor Honors Span Suites and Dining
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Hotel Mulia Senayan in Jakarta has earned multiple Tripadvisor Travelers’ Choice recognitions for 2026, extending across its accommodation and dining experiences. The Suites at Hotel Mulia Senayan received Travelers’ Choice Best of the Best, placing it among the top 1% of properties on Tripadvisor, while the hotel itself ranks among the top 10% of hotels on the platform. The recognition also reaches into the hotel’s culinary portfolio, with Table8 among the top 1% of restaurants worldwide and Edogin, Cascade Lounge, il Mare and The Café among the top 10%.

The breadth of the honors offers a snapshot of what has made Hotel Mulia Senayan a longstanding presence in Jakarta’s luxury hospitality scene. Located in the Senayan district near the Jakarta Convention Center and the city’s only golf course within the city center, the 994-room hotel combines extensive accommodations and event spaces with a notably broad dining program. The Suites, introduced in 2015, add a more personalized layer of hospitality through dedicated butler service and individually tailored details, while the property’s international art collection extends throughout guest rooms and public spaces.

The Curated Take: Rather than recognizing a single standout experience, Tripadvisor’s 2026 honors touch nearly every part of the Hotel Mulia Senayan experience, from its most private accommodations to its restaurants and lounge. For travelers looking at Jakarta through the lens of established luxury, that consistency across such a large property is part of the story.

item.title: 40 Years Later, Crocodile Dundee Still Sends Travelers Into the Australian Outback
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Forty years after Crocodile Dundee arrived in U.S. cinemas, the film’s influence on Australian tourism is still visible in the travelers who follow its trail into the Northern Territory. The 1986 hit transformed the landscapes of Australia into a global backdrop, with Kakadu National Park among its most recognizable locations. The film became the second-highest-grossing movie at the U.S. box office that year, behind Top Gun, while international visitor numbers to Australia doubled to more than two million annually by 1990. Its longer legacy may be the way it helped establish what is now known as set jetting, turning places seen on screen into destinations worth experiencing in person.

Kakadu remains the center of the Crocodile Dundee story, but today’s travelers can experience the landscape beyond the movie set. Self-guided itineraries and 4WD tours revisit locations associated with the film, while Yellow Water cruises offer encounters with saltwater crocodiles, waterbirds and other wildlife on the billabong. Accommodation ranges from the distinctive Crocodile Hotel to Cooinda Lodge, with the wider national park providing access to waterfalls, gorges, wetlands and Indigenous cultural landscapes that give the region its identity beyond its Hollywood connection.

The Curated Take: The enduring “Dundee effect” is an early example of something that has become increasingly powerful in travel: a story can create curiosity about a place, but the landscape has to deliver an experience worth traveling for. In Kakadu, the film provides the starting point, while the wildlife, scale and cultural depth of the Northern Territory give travelers a reason to keep exploring long after the movie reference has faded.

item.title: Bhaya Soul Brings a New Kind of Wellness Journey to Ha Long Bay
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Bhaya Soul has joined Small Luxury Hotels of the World, becoming the collection’s first luxury boat offering in Asia Pacific and adding a new dimension to the way travelers can experience northern Vietnam. The 20-suite wellness cruise moves through Ha Long Bay and Lan Ha Bay along quieter routes, combining private balconies, Vietnamese hospitality, fine dining and an intentionally intimate setting. Rather than treating wellness as a separate amenity, Bhaya Soul builds restoration into the rhythm of the journey, using the surrounding seascape, design, cuisine and nature as part of the experience.

The new SLH membership also creates a potential wellness journey between two very different Vietnamese landscapes. Bhaya Soul can be paired with Namia River Retreat in Hoi An, another SLH property, connecting a floating retreat among the limestone karsts of Ha Long Bay with a river-based experience along the Thu Bon River. Together, the properties offer a way to explore Vietnam through two distinct environments while maintaining a focus on slowing down, reconnecting and experiencing the destination at a more deliberate pace.

The Curated Take: Bhaya Soul is interesting because it challenges the conventional idea of a Ha Long Bay cruise as a sightseeing experience. The landscape remains central, but the emphasis shifts from seeing as much as possible to inhabiting the setting. That approach feels particularly relevant to the evolution of luxury wellness travel, where the destination itself increasingly becomes part of the restoration.

item.title: Redwoods, Coast, and Cabernet
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
This piece is part of the latest issue of Curated Travel Magazine, where we explore travel through immersive stories, cultural insight, and thoughtfully curated experiences around the world.

Tracing Northern California’s dramatic transitions from vine to coast.

Drive thirty minutes west of the Napa Valley floor, and the tidy, sun-drenched grid of cabernet vines gives way to something far raw: dense stands of old-growth redwoods, fog-draped ridges, and the craggy, tide-swept cliffs of the Sonoma Coast. While most visitors treat wine country as a series of stationary tastings, the region is fundamentally defined by these sudden, stark shifts in terrain—best experienced from behind the wheel on a loop through its backroads.

Starting at the southern nexus of Napa and Sonoma, a drive up the historic Silverado Trail offers a quiet alternative to Highway 29. Lined with oak trees and stone-built estates, this two-lane corridor bypasses central valley traffic, connecting rustic tasting rooms in Rutherford with the hot springs and volcanic foothills of Calistoga.

From the valley’s northern tip, a western cut across the Mayacamas Mountains shifts the scenery entirely. As the pavement winds down toward Bodega Bay, the warm air of the valley vanishes, replaced by cool ocean breezes and sweeping Pacific vistas. Further inland, the route dips beneath the towering, light-dappled canopy of Sonoma’s redwood groves, where narrow roads twist through giant sequoias before looping back toward the vines.

Local resorts like Carneros Resort and Spa cater directly to this road-trip culture, offering curated routing guides and vintage or electric vehicle rentals for guests using the property as a regional launchpad. But whether behind the wheel of a classic convertible or a local rental, navigating these interconnected loops proves that Northern California’s true allure lies in the vivid landscapes between the destinations.

item.title: Two Hyatt Culinary Leaders Bring Global Experience to Bali’s Sanur
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Hyatt Regency Bali and Andaz Bali, by Hyatt are entering a new chapter for their food and beverage programs with the appointment of Ivan Gutierrez as Cluster Director of Food & Beverage and Chef Vincenzo Gatti as Cluster Executive Chef. Together, the two leaders bring extensive experience across Hyatt properties in Asia, including Park Hyatt Tokyo, Grand Hyatt Tokyo, Grand Hyatt Seoul and Hyatt Regency Hua Hin, giving the two Sanur resorts a leadership team with a distinctly international perspective on dining and hospitality.

Chef Vincenzo arrives in Bali after serving as Executive Chef at Andaz Pattaya Jomtien Beach, where La Cucina Italian Restaurant and Fish Club Seafood Restaurant received Michelin Guide recognition when the guide launched its Pattaya selection in 2025. Gutierrez, meanwhile, most recently led food and beverage at Grand Hyatt Erawan Bangkok and has held leadership roles across Hyatt properties in Japan, China and Thailand. In their new roles, Gutierrez will oversee food and beverage strategy and service culture across both resorts, while Gatti will lead the culinary direction, with both emphasizing collaboration, talent development and memorable guest experiences.

The Curated Take: The appointments point to an increasingly sophisticated culinary identity for Sanur, where international hospitality expertise can intersect with Bali’s distinctive sense of place. The more interesting question is not simply what new restaurants or menus might emerge, but how these two leaders translate experience gathered across Asia into dining that feels appropriate to Bali and its guests.

item.title: Bellevue Builds a Car-Free Basecamp for Pacific Northwest Adventures
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Bellevue, Washington, is making it easier to experience the Pacific Northwest without a car, with a growing network of shuttles, light rail connections and bike options linking travelers from arrival to outdoor adventure. The expanded Bellevue Airport & Cruise Shuttle connects hotels with Seattle-Tacoma International Airport and Seattle’s cruise terminals, while the new Bellevue Light Rail Shuttle provides free, on-demand electric transportation from the Bellevue Downtown Station to hotels, restaurants, shops and attractions. Ride Bellevue adds another layer, giving visitors access to e-bikes as well as gravel and mountain bikes for exploring the region without bringing their own equipment.

The transportation changes arrive as Bellevue adds new reasons to make the city a base for a Pacific Northwest trip. Nobu Bellevue and Nobu Bellevue Residences are planned for 2027, alongside The Emily Hotel and a new winter festival centered on light, art and seasonal programming. In the Wilburton district, the evolving Eastrail corridor and restoration of the historic Wilburton Trestle will connect visitors to a growing regional trail network. With more than 100 parks and public spaces, Lake Washington shoreline and easy connections to Seattle, Woodinville Wine Country and mountain recreation, Bellevue is positioning itself as a place where urban comfort and the outdoors can be part of the same itinerary.

The Curated Take: Bellevue’s most interesting development may be the connective tissue between its experiences. Rather than requiring travelers to choose between a polished urban stay and access to the Pacific Northwest landscape, the city is building a model around both. For travelers who prefer the ease of a sophisticated home base but still want nature, culture and regional exploration within reach, that changes how Bellevue fits into a Seattle-area itinerary.

item.title: Dunedin and Waitaki Bring New Zealand’s Quirky Side Into Focus
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Dunedin and Waitaki have been named among Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel destinations for 2027, putting one of New Zealand’s most distinctive regional pairings on the global travel map. The only New Zealand destination included in the 2027 edition, the area joins 50 destinations worldwide recognized by the travel guide for the year ahead. Lonely Planet describes Dunedin and nearby Ōamaru as among Aotearoa’s “coolest and quirkiest” corners, where Victorian heritage, creative culture, dramatic coastal landscapes and wildlife come together in unexpected ways.

The character of the region is perhaps best understood through its contrasts. In Dunedin, travelers can move from its arts, restaurant and cocktail scene into green hills, coastal bays and wildlife experiences, while Ōamaru adds its distinctive Victorian whitestone architecture, Steampunk culture and nightly little blue penguin sightings. The wider Waitaki region extends the story into lakes, rivers, open landscapes and the Waitaki Whitestone UNESCO Global Geopark, creating a destination that feels less like a collection of attractions and more like a place with its own unmistakable personality.

The Curated Take: Lonely Planet’s recognition is particularly fitting because Dunedin and Waitaki’s appeal is not built around a single headline attraction. It is the unusual combination of heritage, landscape, wildlife and local creativity that gives the region its identity. For travelers looking beyond New Zealand’s most familiar routes, this is a part of the South Island where the unexpected is part of the experience.
